color.definition.question: How is the palette defined?
color.definition.why: Warm neutrals and one vivid ramp.

accessibility.definition.question: What contrast floor do we hold?
accessibility.definition.why: AA, checked on every vivid color.

spacing.definition.question: How are spacing steps defined?
spacing.definition.why: Big, even steps make big moments.

typography.definition.question: How are sizes and line heights defined?
typography.definition.answer: A ratio, line heights in proportion
typography.definition.why: Ratios suit the big display sizes.

typography.values.question: How large is body text?
typography.values.why: Regular body; the display does the shouting.

shape.definition.question: How are corners set?
shape.definition.why: One brand, one set of corners.

elevation.definition.question: What separates groups on the page?

motion.definition.question: How is easing defined?
motion.definition.why: A spring that overshoots feels alive.

motion.values.question: How fast does feedback feel?
motion.values.why: Feedback stays fast; the personality shows in panels and hero moments, which move slower on a spring.

accessibility.values.question: What is the smallest target?
accessibility.values.why: Visitors come from social posts on phones.

content.q1.question: What is the main content?
content.q1.why: Images, campaigns and short punchy copy.

business.q1.question: What does the product do for the business?
business.q1.why: A launch site that must win attention and sign-ups.

brand.q1.question: What should the brand feel like?

brand.q2.question: How visible is the brand in the interface?

accessibility.roles.question: Which states get their own visible value?

scenarios.q1.question: Where do people use it?
scenarios.q1.why: Visitors come from social posts on their phones.

people.q1.question: Who uses it most?
people.q1.why: New customers deciding if they care.

people.q2.question: What accessibility level do we commit to?

motion.count.question: How many speeds exist?
motion.count.why: Fast feedback, moderate panels, relaxed hero.

motion.lands.question: Where does motion show?
motion.lands.why: Motion shows in hero and launch moments.

brand.q3.question: Which typefaces carry the product, and why?
brand.q3.answer: A display face for brand moments, with a sans for text
brand.q3.why: Bricolage Grotesque for display and headings, DM Sans for text: loud where the brand speaks, easy where people read.

typography.roles.question: Which text roles does it need?
typography.roles.why: A big expressive display role carries the brand.

content.q2.question: How much is on one screen?

tasks.q2.question: How often do people repeat actions?

voice.lands.question: Where do the words matter most?
voice.lands.why: Words work hardest in headlines and buttons.

typography.count.question: How many steps does the type scale take?
typography.count.answer: Fine steps, so pages can set their own rhythm
typography.count.why: Fine steps give big moments room.

typography.lands.question: Where does type do the most work?
typography.lands.why: Type does its work in headlines.

shape.roles.question: Which shape roles does it need?
shape.roles.why: Pills everywhere; badges share the control corner.

shape.count.question: How many corner sizes exist?
shape.count.why: Pill controls and large container corners.

elevation.roles.question: What rises above the page?
elevation.roles.why: Cards lift to feel like objects.

theming.values.question: Which modes ship?
theming.values.why: Light and dark ship as standard.

iconography.values.question: How big are icons next to text?
iconography.values.why: Larger icons hold their own next to big type.

iconography.count.question: How many icon sizes exist?
iconography.count.why: One size next to text, one for decoration.

spacing.roles.question: Which spacing roles does it need?
spacing.roles.why: Few tables; no row role needed.

color.count.question: How many emphasis levels do actions need?

accessibility.count.question: How many signals carry each meaning?

color.lands.question: Where does color carry meaning first?

outcomes.q2.question: What is a costly mistake?
outcomes.q2.why: A bland page is the costly mistake.

border-width.default.why: We use a 2px default line for card borders in order to give grouping in a bold tone. A heavier stroke does this by drawing a shared region with the weight of the bold type beside it. So each card holds its offer next to vivid color, because cards separate groups (elevation.definition), AA holds on every color (accessibility.definition) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

focus.ring.offset.why: We use a fixed 2px focus offset in order to keep focus visible by contrast, not for style. The gap does this by showing the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps enough contrast against any fill (W3C technique C40). So visitors see the ring on any brand color, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles).
focus.ring.offset.description: The gap between a control and its focus ring, so the ring never touches the control and reads on any fill.

focus.ring.width.why: We use a 3px focus ring in order to show focus, one step heavier than the 2px default line by the focus relation. A heavier stroke does this by standing out even from the bold edges around it. So keyboard users see focus on vivid color, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles) and AA holds on every color (accessibility.definition).
focus.ring.width.description: The focus ring's width: one step heavier than the default border, and not a border width.

motion.duration.feedback.why: We use 120ms (fast) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to answer each tap at once, well inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the finger lifts. So visitors feel the brand respond, never lag, because motion carries expression (motion.roles) and feedback feels fast (motion.values).
motion.duration.feedback.description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

motion.duration.exit.why: We use 120ms (fast) for a layer that closes in order to end the exit move faster than the 200ms open. The duration does this by removing what people are done with in fewer frames than it took to arrive. So visitors get back to the page at once, because even an expressive family keeps exits short (motion.roles) and there are three speeds (motion.count).
motion.duration.exit.description: A layer closing: shorter than its open.

motion.duration.panels.why: We use 200ms (moderate) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by giving the eye time to follow the panel from its trigger. So visitors see each menu arrive as part of the brand, because the family is expressive (motion.roles) and there are three speeds (motion.count).
motion.duration.panels.description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

motion.duration.hero.why: We use 320ms (relaxed) for hero and launch moments in order to give the slowest move to the moment that matters most, inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by holding the change long enough to be seen as an event. So every visitor sees the launch, because motion shows in hero moments (motion.lands) and the family is expressive (motion.roles).
motion.duration.hero.description: Hero and launch moments. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

motion.easing.exit-offscreen.why: We use the accelerate easing (0.4, 0, 1, 1) for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen in order to do the exit move of a layer that leaves the view. The curve does this by starting slow and speeding up, so the panel gathers pace on its way out. So visitors read the drawer as gone, not paused at the edge, because an expressive family accelerates only what leaves the screen (motion.roles) and easing is set per move (motion.definition).
motion.easing.exit-offscreen.description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

motion.easing.emphasize.why: We use the spring easing (0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) for the emphasize move only, in order to celebrate a moment such as a sign-up that worked. The curve does this by passing its target and settling back, so the eye catches the bounce. So the brand's spring is felt where it means something, not on every menu, because easing is a spring (motion.definition) and motion carries expression (motion.roles).
motion.easing.emphasize.description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention. The only move that overshoots.

motion.easing.standard.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move without the spring. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling, with no overshoot. So buttons and toggles feel quick and steady, and the bounce stays special, because the spring is for emphasis only (motion.definition) in an expressive family (motion.roles).
motion.easing.standard.description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

motion.easing.enter.why: We use the standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So a menu is readable almost as soon as it opens, because an expressive family keeps its spring for emphasis (motion.roles) and enters on an ease-out (motion.definition).
motion.easing.enter.description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

motion.easing.exit.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next tap, because an expressive exit eases out unless the layer leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is set per move (motion.definition).
motion.easing.exit.description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

type.heading.font-size.why: Heading sets 28px, the smallest headline step, so it carries the display face into cards and dialogs without competing with the hero.

type.title.font-size.why: Title sets 40px, one step below display, so the sign-up form's title stays big and keeps the form in view on a phone.

type.display.font-size.why: Display sets 56px, the largest step, because every hero opens with one big idea in the brand's loudest voice.

type.body.font-weight.why: Body stays at weight 400, regular, because the display does the shouting and the text only has to read.

type.caption.font-weight.why: Captions stay at weight 400, regular, so fine print never pulls the eye from the bold headlines.

type.data.font-weight.why: Data stays at weight 400, regular DM Sans, so numbers in short copy keep the brand's text voice.

type.heading.font-weight.why: Heading drops to weight 700, one step under display and title, so cards stay bold without shouting over the hero.

type.label.font-weight.why: Labels set weight 700, bold DM Sans, so a field label holds on vivid color and matches the bold brand.

type.display.font-weight.why: Display sets weight 800, the heaviest step, because the hero headline carries the bold, loud brand.

type.title.font-weight.why: Title keeps weight 800 from display, so the form page still speaks in the brand's bold headline voice.

radius.element.why: We use the 12px box corner for boxes that grow in order to keep them box-shaped objects by the relation: a pill control gives way to the box corner. A moderate radius does this by curving the corners while the sides stay straight as the box grows. So a text area or a list item stays a box, not an oval, because controls are pills (shape.values) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).
radius.element.description: Corner of an element that holds content and can grow past one line: a list item, an accordion row, a text area, a calendar, an attachment, a skeleton or media.

radius.option.why: We use a 20px corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 24px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because surfaces take 24px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).
radius.option.description: Corner of options in menus and lists: the panel's corner less its padding, so the corners nest.

radius.surface.why: We use a 24px corner for cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each offer read as a separate object, in a bold tone by brand convention. A large radius does this by breaking the outline with a wide curve while the sides stay straight. So each offer reads as one friendly object, because containers get their own corner (shape.count) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).
radius.surface.description: Corner of cards, menus and dialogs.

radius.control.why: We use a pill corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a playful tone, by brand convention. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule, the brand's signature shape. So every action feels bold and friendly, because the brand is bold (brand.q1), controls are pills (shape.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

radius.badge.why: We use the pill control corner for badges in order to keep one role family by the badge relation: badges share the control's corner. The same full radius does this by giving a status the capsule of the buttons beside it. So a status pill matches the buttons and the page keeps one shape, because badges get no corner of their own (shape.roles) and controls are pills (shape.values).
radius.badge.description: Corner of badges, chips, tooltips, keyboard keys (kbd) and checkboxes: small labels and marks.

elevation.card.why: We use step 1 of the shadow scale for cards in order to show their height as objects above the page. The cast shade does this by a 12px offset and a 32px blur at 14%. So each offer feels like an object you can pick up, because cards rise too (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).

elevation.overlay.why: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show floating height, one step above the cards. The cast shade does this by a 24px offset and a 48px blur at 20%, larger than the card's. So a menu sits clearly above vivid sections and cards, because cards and overlays rise (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).

size.icon.why: Icons beside text are 20px, larger than the 17px body, so they hold their own next to big type.

size.control.compact.why: We use 44px for compact controls, such as a button inside a pill field, in order to make a hit target: one 8px step below the 52px default on the control scale, a 44px hit area that still fits a thumb. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So a button sits inside the pill field and still fits a thumb, because visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

size.hit-area.why: We use a 44px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a checkbox, a radio or a switch, in order to make a hit target a fingertip can find: the WCAG 2.5.5 size. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, and rows in a group stand at least 44px apart, so no two targets overlap. So visitors tap the right control on a phone, because targets are sized for touch (accessibility.values) and the layout leaves room for it (spacing.values).
size.hit-area.description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

size.control.default.why: We use 52px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the touch target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 52px hit area. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So every control fits a thumb, because the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values) and visitors arrive on their phones (scenarios.q1).
size.control.default.description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

size.row.why: We use 52px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: by inheritance, as the scheme has no row role and a row holds controls, so size.row takes size.control.default, one 52px control tall. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So the rare table keeps the brand's airy rhythm, because spacing has gaps and insets only (spacing.roles) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

size.control.large.why: We use 60px for the one loud call to action in order to make a hit target: one 8px step above the 52px default on the control scale, a 60px hit area, as sign-up is the scheme's hero action. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So the sign-up button wins the eye and the thumb, because there is one action, sign up (tasks.q2), and visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1).
size.control.large.description: Height of large controls: the one loud call to action.

space.gap.default.why: We use 16px for the default gap between the items of one group in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 8px), twice the tight gap. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So air between items keeps big type readable, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and delight is the point (human.q1).

space.inset.cell-x.why: We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: two base steps (2 × 8px), the same as the default gap. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So the rare table keeps the page's airy rhythm, because the content is images and campaigns, with few tables (content.q1), and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

component-spacing-map.hairline.why: hairline: A fixed 2px optical nudge, the same in every scheme. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.
component-spacing-map.hairline.description: A fixed 2px optical nudge, the same in every scheme.

component-spacing-map.x3.why: x3: 3 × the base step, times the rhythm 2, so it is space.24. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

space.inset.control-x.why: We use 28px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: three and a half base steps (3.5 × 8px), wider than a table cell. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So pill buttons look bold and are easy to hit with a thumb, because the brand is bold (brand.q1) and visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1).

better.name: label side padding on touch screens

space.inset.container.why: We use 32px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: four base steps (4 × 8px), twice the default gap. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So each card holds its moment, because delight is the point (human.q1) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

component-spacing-map.x4.why: x4: 4 × the base step, times the rhythm 2, so it is space.32. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

component-spacing-map.x1.why: x1: 1 × the base step, held at every rhythm, so it is space.4. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

space.gap.group.why: We use 40px for the group gap between groups inside a section in order to group and separate: five base steps (5 × 8px), two and a half default gaps. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So each group has its own moment inside a section, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

component-spacing-map.x6.why: x6: 6 × the base step, times the rhythm 2, so it is space.48. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

space.gap.section.why: We use 64px for the section gap between big sections in order to group and separate: eight base steps (8 × 8px), four default gaps. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So each section, with its color block, is a moment of its own, because space works between big sections (spacing.lands) and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

component-spacing-map.x8.why: x8: 8 × the base step, times the rhythm 2, so it is space.64. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

component-spacing-map.x12.why: x12: 12 × the base step, times the rhythm 2, so it is space.64. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

space.gap.tight.why: We use 8px for the tight gap between the parts of one item, such as an icon and its word, in order to group and separate: one base step (1 × 8px), the smallest of the big even steps. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So a call to action reads as one bold unit, because steps are big and even (spacing.definition) and the content is images and campaigns (content.q1).

component-spacing-map.x2.why: x2: 2 × the base step, held at every rhythm, so it is space.8. Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

color.surface.highlight.why: We use a step darker than content for the item under the pointer or the keyboard in dark, in order to mark it as a band on both surfaces it meets: 1.08:1 on surface.default and 1.31:1 on surface.raised. The fill does this by stepping darker, as raised layers took the lighter step; muted text still reads 7.26:1 on it. So the hovered row or menu item shows on cards and menus alike, because hover and focus have their own look (accessibility.roles) and the neutral ramp sets the steps (color.definition).
color.surface.highlight.description: The item the pointer or the keyboard is on.
